questions.q: What message does the editorial read in the election of a bus driver’s son as Mayor of London?
options: Opportunities are now open to all who work for merit by peaceful means; complaint should give way to positive planning
Yes. “Making the impossible possible.”
Politics is the only road to progress
Not quite. The article says: Opportunities are now open to all who work for merit by peaceful means; complaint should give way to positive planning.
Success depends on family connections
Not quite. The article says: Opportunities are now open to all who work for merit by peaceful means; complaint should give way to positive planning.
London is unlike every other city
Not quite. The article says: Opportunities are now open to all who work for merit by peaceful means; complaint should give way to positive planning.
questions.rationale: “Abandon thinking along the lines of complaint and make plans for actions on a positive basis… Their goal should be to achieve competence and be meritorious.”

questions.article: The Relationship Between Fasting and Life
questions.q: The Islamic creed begins with “There is no god” before “but God.” What general pattern does the article see in this?
options: Denial matters more than belief
Not quite. The article says: Half of what is asked of us is to abstain and half to act – and fasting trains the abstaining.
Every statement should begin with a negative
Not quite. The article says: Half of what is asked of us is to abstain and half to act – and fasting trains the abstaining.
Half of what is asked of us is to abstain and half to act – and fasting trains the abstaining
Right. It is the “brake” that makes the journey safe.
Words matter more than deeds
Not quite. The article says: Half of what is asked of us is to abstain and half to act – and fasting trains the abstaining.
questions.rationale: “There is a 50:50 ratio in all the actions man has to perform in life i.e. 50% of the actions require abstaining from something and the other 50% acting on something.”

questions.article: The Importance of Religion in Peace Building
questions.q: According to the article, which part of religion gives rise to conflict between communities, and which does not?
options: Charity causes conflict; prayer does not
Not quite. The article says: Insistence on outward form causes clashes; the inner spirit – truthfulness, honesty, goodwill – does not.
Scripture causes conflict; custom does not
Not quite. The article says: Insistence on outward form causes clashes; the inner spirit – truthfulness, honesty, goodwill – does not.
Belief causes conflict; ritual does not
Not quite. The article says: Insistence on outward form causes clashes; the inner spirit – truthfulness, honesty, goodwill – does not.
Insistence on outward form causes clashes; the inner spirit – truthfulness, honesty, goodwill – does not
Yes. Spirit is the real part; form calls for tolerance.
questions.rationale: “The spiritual content of religion does not create any problem. The problem is always created by the form of the religion. When the form is emphasized, differences, clash and confrontation ensue.”

questions.article: The Importance of Religion in Peace Building
questions.q: The article notes that in business a “customer-friendly” culture is adopted. What does it say is the essence of the social teaching of every religion?
options: A human-friendly culture – goodwill towards all, even opponents
Well read. “Follow one and respect all.”
A culture of silence
Not quite. The article says: A human-friendly culture – goodwill towards all, even opponents.
A culture of competition
Not quite. The article says: A human-friendly culture – goodwill towards all, even opponents.
A culture of separation
Not quite. The article says: A human-friendly culture – goodwill towards all, even opponents.
questions.rationale: “Similarly the essence of the social teachings of every religion is a human-friendly culture.”

questions.q: How does the article distinguish seeking wealth for one’s needs from seeking it for its own sake?
options: Needs grow with age; greed fades
Not quite. The article says: Needs have a limit and can be satisfied; wealth as an aim has none, so contentment never comes.
Both end in contentment
Not quite. The article says: Needs have a limit and can be satisfied; wealth as an aim has none, so contentment never comes.
Needs have a limit and can be satisfied; wealth as an aim has none, so contentment never comes
Correct. “Greed for more and more distracted you… till you reached the grave.”
Neither can ever be satisfied
Not quite. The article says: Needs have a limit and can be satisfied; wealth as an aim has none, so contentment never comes.
questions.rationale: “If it is to meet your needs that you seek wealth, when you have earned enough to meet your needs you will be content. But if you have made acquiring wealth for its own sake your life’s purpose, you will never be content.”

questions.q: What does the article say an iftar gathering ought to be?
options: A competition in cooking
Not quite. The article says: An occasion for spiritual exchange, turning a private experience into a shared one.
An occasion for spiritual exchange, turning a private experience into a shared one
Yes. Not a party like any other.
A meeting to discuss business
Not quite. The article says: An occasion for spiritual exchange, turning a private experience into a shared one.
A display of the host’s generosity
Not quite. The article says: An occasion for spiritual exchange, turning a private experience into a shared one.
questions.rationale: “Such a party should give us an opportunity for spiritual exchange, turning our individual experience into a social experience.”

questions.q: On waking each morning the Prophet would say, “All praise and thanks are due to God who gave us life after death.” What does this teach, according to the article?
options: Mornings are the best time for prayer
Not quite. The article says: Sleeping and waking are daily reminders of death and of rising again to give account.
Sleeping and waking are daily reminders of death and of rising again to give account
Right. Ordinary acts become reminders of the Hereafter.
Sleep is a kind of illness
Not quite. The article says: Sleeping and waking are daily reminders of death and of rising again to give account.
Dreams foretell the future
Not quite. The article says: Sleeping and waking are daily reminders of death and of rising again to give account.
questions.rationale: “Going to sleep is like dying and waking up in the morning is like rising from the grave.”

questions.q: Why, in the article’s account, does true faith lead a person to simplicity?
options: Because others expect it of him
Not quite. The article says: Having seen God’s greatness he feels his own smallness, and modesty shows in how he lives.
Having seen God’s greatness he feels his own smallness, and modesty shows in how he lives
Yes. “Simplicity is undoubtedly a part of faith.”
Because he can no longer afford comfort
Not quite. The article says: Having seen God’s greatness he feels his own smallness, and modesty shows in how he lives.
Because luxury is forbidden to all
Not quite. The article says: Having seen God’s greatness he feels his own smallness, and modesty shows in how he lives.
questions.rationale: “When man has discovered the greatness of God, his own existence in comparison appears quite insignificant… All this inevitably results in his preferring simplicity in everything.”

questions.q: What does the article say a person gains who has truly found God, when he suffers a loss?
options: Indifference to other people
Not quite. The article says: A conviction that his greatest asset, God, is still with him – so loss no longer breaks him.
A conviction that his greatest asset, God, is still with him – so loss no longer breaks him
Exactly. Adversity brings its own good tidings.
Freedom from ever losing again
Not quite. The article says: A conviction that his greatest asset, God, is still with him – so loss no longer breaks him.
A promise that losses will be repaid at once
Not quite. The article says: A conviction that his greatest asset, God, is still with him – so loss no longer breaks him.
questions.rationale: “Losses no longer matter; he never loses the feeling that his greatest asset, God, is still with him.”

questions.q: The Prophet said the fasting person has two delights. What are they?
options: One at breaking the fast, the other at meeting his Lord
Well read. The first is a foretaste of the second.
One at dawn, the other at noon
Not quite. The article says: One at breaking the fast, the other at meeting his Lord.
One in youth, the other in old age
Not quite. The article says: One at breaking the fast, the other at meeting his Lord.
One in giving, the other in receiving
Not quite. The article says: One at breaking the fast, the other at meeting his Lord.
questions.rationale: “The fasting person has two delights: one at the time of breaking the fast and the other at the time of meeting with his Lord God most High.”
